Gastric acid challenge and surface sealant agents: Their impact on the optical 
and mechanical integrity of denture base materials.

STATEMENT OF PROBLEM: Denture base resins are subject to chemical and mechanical 
stressors in the oral environment that may compromise their structural 
integrity. Among these, exposure to acidic conditions-originating from dietary 
sources, medications, or gastric reflux-can adversely affect surface properties. 
Considering the clinical relevance of these alterations, evaluating surface 
roughness, hardness, and gloss is essential for understanding the performance 
and durability of dental materials.
PURPOSE: The aim of this in vitro study was to assess the effect of simulated 
gastric acid exposure on the gloss, microhardness, and surface roughness of 
denture base materials fabricated by different techniques and subjected to 
various surface treatments.
MATERIAL AND METHODS: A total of 108 disk-shaped specimens were fabricated using 
3 techniques: conventional heat-polymerization, subtractive manufacturing, and 
additive manufacturing. Each group was subdivided according to surface 
treatment: conventional polishing (control), Optiglaze, or Palaseal coating 
agent application. The specimens were immersed in simulated gastric acid for 
24 hours, simulating 2 years of clinical exposure. Gloss (GU), microhardness 
(VHN), and surface roughness (Ra) were measured before and after immersion, and 
changes (∆GU, ∆VHN, ∆Ra) were calculated. Data were analyzed using 2-way ANOVA 
with the Tukey post hoc test, and correlations were assessed with the Pearson 
test (α=.05).
RESULTS: Simulated gastric acid exposure resulted in decreased microhardness, 
increased surface roughness, and reduced gloss across all groups. The 
heat-polymerized and subtractive specimens exhibited significantly smaller ∆Ra 
and ∆VHN values than the additive group (P<.001). Gloss loss (∆GU) was greater 
in additive and subtractive groups compared with heat-polymerized specimens. The
